power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Unobtrusive recognition of activities of daily living (ADLs) from ambient sensors may support longitudinal assessment of everyday functioning in adults with mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD).
However, real-world activity recognition is complicated by heterogeneous home layouts, sensor configurations, routines, and class distributions.

Objective: This study evaluated whether a room-aware Transformer that preserves locationspecific sensor structure improves participant-level ADL recognition relative to a global Transformer and a stacked unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network.
Methods: Following pilot feasibility testing with two adult volunteers, we analyzed five homes of adults with mild NCD, comprising 92,765 minute-level observations across 67 annotated home-days.
Motion, temperature, illuminance, humidity, and door-contact data were aligned to participant activity logs.
The original labels were harmonized into eight categories.
Models were developed separately for each home using 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows.
Complete calendar days were assigned to mutually exclusive training, validation, and chronological test sets, and no sequence crossed a day or partition boundary.
The same partitions and evaluation procedures were used for all three architectures.
Performance was assessed on held-out test days using accuracy, per-class F1 score, and micro-and macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
Results: The room-aware Transformer achieved the highest or tied accuracy in 9 of 15 homewindow comparisons.
Its accuracy ranged from 0.27 to 0.57, micro-AUC from 0.57 to 0.82, and macro-AUC from 0.54 to 0.78.
Across the 15 settings, mean accuracy was similar for the roomaware and global Transformers and higher than for the LSTM.
Mean micro-AUC and macro-AUC were marginally higher for the global Transformer than for the room-aware Transformer.
The room-aware model showed its clearest gains in selected contexts, including Homes C and E at 10 minutes and Home A at 60 minutes, but no architecture or temporal window was uniformly optimal.
Sleep/Rest was the most consistently recognized activity, whereas low-support activities frequently had low F1 scores despite moderate or high AUC values.
Conclusions: Room-specific feature processing provided context-dependent gains in participantlevel ADL classification, particularly for accuracy in several home-window settings.

The marked variation across homes, activities, and temporal windows supports personalized model development, class-sensitive evaluation, and validation in larger and more diverse residential samples before clinical use.

Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD) is characterized by a modest decline in one or more cognitive domains beyond that expected with normal aging, while independence in everyday activities remains generally preserved [1].
text.formatted: Mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD) is characterized by a modest decline in one or more cognitive domains beyond that expected with normal aging, while independence in everyday activities remains generally preserved <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Mild NCD substantially overlaps with the mild cognitive impairment (MCI), which is commonly described as an intermediate state between normal cognitive aging and dementia [2].
text.formatted: Mild NCD substantially overlaps with the mild cognitive impairment (MCI), which is commonly described as an intermediate state between normal cognitive aging and dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: For some individuals, mild NCD may represent an early point along the Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) clinical continuum.

Although substantial functional dependence is not characteristic of mild NCD, individuals may require greater effort, additional time, compensatory strategies, or accommodations to complete complex daily activities [1].
text.formatted: Although substantial functional dependence is not characteristic of mild NCD, individuals may require greater effort, additional time, compensatory strategies, or accommodations to complete complex daily activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, unobtrusive recognition of activities of daily living using ambient sensors may help characterize subtle functional patterns and longitudinal changes within natural home environments.
Early detection and tracking of such functional decline is critical for timely intervention.

Moreover, recognition of changes in ADL performance may aid in early diagnosis, as subtle changes in routine motion patterns, sleep-wake cycles, and household behaviors often precede clinically detected deterioration by months or even years [3].
text.formatted: Moreover, recognition of changes in ADL performance may aid in early diagnosis, as subtle changes in routine motion patterns, sleep-wake cycles, and household behaviors often precede clinically detected deterioration by months or even years <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: However, traditional assessment methods rely on infrequent clinical visits or caregiver reports, which can be subjective, inconsistent, and unable to capture real-world activity patterns [5].
text.formatted: However, traditional assessment methods rely on infrequent clinical visits or caregiver reports, which can be subjective, inconsistent, and unable to capture real-world activity patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Low-cost sensors, such as motion, temperature, luminance, and door-contact devices, provide rich temporal signals that may capture ADL performance while preserving privacy and avoiding adherence challenges common to other methods (e.g., cameras, wearable devices) [4].
text.formatted: Low-cost sensors, such as motion, temperature, luminance, and door-contact devices, provide rich temporal signals that may capture ADL performance while preserving privacy and avoiding adherence challenges common to other methods (e.g., cameras, wearable devices) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, in-home ambient sensors have gained growing attention in biomedical informatics due to their unobtrusive nature, scalability, and ability to capture minute-level activity sequences.

Prior work using motion sensors, door-contact sensors, and environmental readings demonstrated potential for early detection of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and functional change among older adults [5] [6].
text.formatted: Prior work using motion sensors, door-contact sensors, and environmental readings demonstrated potential for early detection of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and functional change among older adults <ref type="bibr">[5] [6]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, artificial intelligence (AI) models have shown promise for classifying ADLs, but many require dense instrumentation, large training sets, or computationally heavy architectures that limit practical deployment in real homes.
Deep Learning sequence models for ADL recognition may overcome some of these limitations, as they can yield high classification accuracy with lower instrumentation and sample size needs.
For example, Liciotti et al reported 66.92 -94.12% accuracy for ADL recognition with LSTM-based models developed from the CASAS datasets [7].
text.formatted: For example, Liciotti et al reported 66.92 -94.12% accuracy for ADL recognition with LSTM-based models developed from the CASAS datasets <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, across five CASAS homes, Srivatsa and Plötz reported F1-scores of 0.746 to 0.901 for LSTM, 0.755 to 0.904 for transformer, and 0.783 to 0.924 for bidirectional LSTM [8].
text.formatted: Similarly, across five CASAS homes, Srivatsa and Plötz reported F1-scores of 0.746 to 0.901 for LSTM, 0.755 to 0.904 for transformer, and 0.783 to 0.924 for bidirectional LSTM <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, Addepalli et al. proposed a deterministic room-specialized mixture-of-experts architecture that routed activity segments to compact room-specific transformer experts, achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.60-0.88 across five naturally occupied homes [9].
text.formatted: Finally, Addepalli et al. proposed a deterministic room-specialized mixture-of-experts architecture that routed activity segments to compact room-specific transformer experts, achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.60-0.88 across five naturally occupied homes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these results suggest that deep sequence predictive models can accurately and efficiently recognize ADLs from heterogeneous sensor streams.
Of course, there were important methodological variations in how sensory data was represented spatially and temporally across these studies.
Liciotti et al applied unidirectional and bidirectional LSTMs to globally represented CASAS sensor sequences, capturing temporal dependencies without explicitly preserving room-level structure [7].
text.formatted: Liciotti et al applied unidirectional and bidirectional LSTMs to globally represented CASAS sensor sequences, capturing temporal dependencies without explicitly preserving room-level structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Srivatsa and Plötz instead modeled sensors as a learned graph based on co-activation relationships, encoding local and global sensor dependencies without organizing features into functional room-specific branches [8].
text.formatted: Srivatsa and Plötz instead modeled sensors as a learned graph based on co-activation relationships, encoding local and global sensor dependencies without organizing features into functional room-specific branches <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: And the room-specialized mixture of experts used deterministic hard gating to route each activity segment to a single independently trained room expert [9].
text.formatted: And the room-specialized mixture of experts used deterministic hard gating to route each activity segment to a single independently trained room expert <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Unlike these previous studies, our investigation evaluated ADL classification in five heterogeneous, naturally occupied homes of adults with mild NCD.

The proposed room-aware Transformer preserves spatial structure through dedicated room-specific feature projections followed by shared temporal self-attention, and its contribution is examined through comparisons with both a global Transformer and an LSTM baseline.

Moreover, the study evaluates 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows representing recent actions, room-transition patterns, and broader daily routines, respectively, using strictly chronological held-out complete days and both aggregate and class-sensitive performance measures.

Despite these advances, there remains a critical need for efficient, non-invasive ADL recognition systems that can operate reliably in multi-occupant households and accommodate the sparse, noisy nature of real-world sensor data.
This study makes three principal contributions: 1.

It introduces a room-aware Transformer that organizes ambient-sensor features by functional location and applies room-specific projections before shared temporal selfattention, thereby preserving spatial structure that global representations may obscure.

It evaluates the room-aware Transformer against global Transformer and stacked unidirectional LSTM baselines using 92,765 minute-level observations from five heterogeneous, real-world homes of adults with mild NCD, capturing variation in layouts, sensor configurations, activity distributions, and routines.
It examines 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows representing recent actions, room transitions, and broader daily routines, respectively.
The observed variation across homes indicates that temporal-context selection should account for household-specific activity patterns, rather than assume a universally optimal window.
We used a two-phase design.
Phase I was a feasibility and development study conducted in one home with two adult volunteers.
Phase II was a real-world model development and evaluation study conducted in five instrumented homes.
The two phases used the same general sensing philosophy and sequence-modeling framework but differed in participant population, household configuration and annotation ontology.
For this reason, data were analyzed by phase and home, rather than pooled as if all minute-level observations were independent and interchangeable.
The University of Missouri Institutional Review Board reviewed and approved the study procedures (IRB #2101666).
All participants, or legally authorized representatives when applicable, and participating caregivers completed the informed consent process before data collection.
The sensing system did not use cameras or microphones.
Sensor and activity-log data were transmitted through encrypted connections and stored on secure institutional systems, and analyses used study identifiers rather than direct personal identifiers.
For both phases, this study utilized a non-wearable, in-home ambient sensing platform designed to capture continuous patterns of daily activity.
The system consisted of multifunction sensors measuring motion, temperature, humidity and luminance, along with door-contact sensors capturing entry and exit events.
All devices communicated through a Raspberry Pi 4 equipped with an Aeotec Z-Stick to enable local data collection and wireless connectivity.

Sensors were placed in key functional areas of the homes, such as the kitchen, living room, bedroom, and bathroom, to monitor movement signals and environmental changes in light, temperature and humidity relevant to ADLs.

The Raspberry Pi, running the OpenHAB homeautomation framework [10], transmitted encrypted data feeds to a secure cloud server via a dedicated Wi-Fi hotspot that can be extracted from API-driven front-end.
text.formatted: The Raspberry Pi, running the OpenHAB homeautomation framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, transmitted encrypted data feeds to a secure cloud server via a dedicated Wi-Fi hotspot that can be extracted from API-driven front-end.

text.text: All sensor data underwent preprocessing and synchronization procedures prior to training the deep learning models used for ADL classification.
The sensing platform, developed by the University of Missouri [11], has been implemented across multiple aging-in-place research sites in Missouri.
text.formatted: The sensing platform, developed by the University of Missouri <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, has been implemented across multiple aging-in-place research sites in Missouri.

text.text: The study datasets comprised five participant dyads enrolled in the AARG study, labeled as Home A, B, C, D and E each consisting of a participant with Mild Neurocognitive Disorder (NCD) and their informal caregiver.
Participants across the five homes ranged in age from 60 to 80 years and had diagnoses of mild NCD between 2022 and 2023 and were enrolled with a clinical diagnosis of mild neurocognitive disorder.
Continuous ambient sensor monitoring was conducted following enrollment, and the baseline diagnosis was used to characterize the study population.
Dyads were White, non-Hispanic and lived in private homes instrumented with the ambient sensing system.
Activity annotations for the participant with mild NCD were used as target labels.
Homes were selected based on the availability of continuous ambient sensor streams, coupled with dense activity annotations to support the training and evaluation of deep learning models.
The input features used for models training were derived directly from the ambient sensing system deployed in the homes of five participants with mild NCD.
The study sensing system contained three types of ambient sensors to capture heterogeneous behavioral and environmental signals.
First, multifunction sensors recorded passive infrared motion events together with continuous light and temperature measurements across primary home locations.

Second, the multisensor provided the same motion, light, and temperature streams while additionally capturing humidity, and were therefore exclusively placed in main bathrooms to capture humidity fluctuations indicative of showering or other hygiene-related activities.
Third, contact door sensors were installed on entry points (e.g., front and garage doors) to capture open-close events associated with household transitions.

Accordingly, the collected data were structured into two main types: binary event data (motion and door states, encoded as 0 in events of no-motion or door closure or 1 if motion detected or door open) derived from all three sensor types, and continuous environmental data (temperature, light, and humidity) obtained from the multifunction and multisensor devices.

Motion events were captured in an event-driven manner, whereas temperature, humidity and illuminance were reported either at fixed default intervals (temperature every 15 minutes; illuminance every 60 minutes) or when the device registered a predefined threshold change (≥1 °C for temperature; ~200 lux for illuminance).
The supervised learning target variable consisted of 13 labeled Activities of Daily Living (ADLs).
To ensure clinical alignment with established functional assessment frameworks, these activities were organized into three groups.

Basic ADLs were defined according to the Katz Index [12], included four ADLs: Toileting, Hygiene, Eating, and Dressing, which reflect fundamental self-care abilities essential for personal hygiene, nutrition, and autonomy.
text.formatted: Basic ADLs were defined according to the Katz Index <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, included four ADLs: Toileting, Hygiene, Eating, and Dressing, which reflect fundamental self-care abilities essential for personal hygiene, nutrition, and autonomy.

text.text: Instrumental ADLs (IADLs) followed the Lawton-Brody Scale [13] and comprised five ADLs: Medication, Cooking, Washing Dishes, Transportation (ability to travel outside the home for errands, appointments, or social activities), and Household activities.
text.formatted: Instrumental ADLs (IADLs) followed the Lawton-Brody Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and comprised five ADLs: Medication, Cooking, Washing Dishes, Transportation (ability to travel outside the home for errands, appointments, or social activities), and Household activities.

text.text: The remaining four ADLs: Sleep/Rest, Mobility (movement within house limit), Leisure/Social activity, and No Activity were categorized as Recreational/Other activities to avoid conflation with clinically validated ADL and IADL measures.
No Activity was operationalized as time intervals in which no activity was logged by the participant, potentially reflecting sedentary or unreported behavior.

Activity annotation for Homes A, B, C, D and E was derived from detailed activity logs completed by the participants and their informal caregivers.
Activity logs captured the day date, start time, end time, activity label, location, and additional notes, enabling temporal alignment with ambient sensor streams.
Both individuals received structured templates and written instructions developed by the MU research team, and informed consent was obtained prior to data collection.
Participants and caregivers documented daily activities three days per week (two weekdays and one weekend day).
The raw activity logs were coded and mapped to the 13 core ADLs described in the previous section.
Follow-up interviews with the participants and caregivers were conducted to clarify activity patterns, validate interpretations, and refine the final target labels used for model evaluation.
Final ADL target labels were aligned to a 24-hour timeline.
The final datasets comprised location-based sensor features and target labels for participants with mild NCD.

Home A contained 27,046 observations and 24 features collected over 20 days, Home B contained 13,860 observations and 21 features collected over 11 days, Home C contained 23,040 observations and 15 features collected over 16 days, Home D contained 12,960 observations and 21 features collected over 9 days, and Home E contained 15,859 observations and 21 features collected over 11 days.
In total, we collected 92,765 minutelevel observations across 67 home-days.

Differences in dimensionality reflect variations in home layouts, monitored locations, and sensor configurations, whereas differences in sample size primarily reflect differences in monitoring duration and data availability across homes.

text.text: Phase I used ambient-sensor data from two adult volunteers to compare stacked LSTM and global transformer models.
Phase II extended the framework to five homes of adults with mild NCD, using location-based preprocessing and the proposed room-aware transformer.
Models were evaluated with 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows using temporally partitioned training, validation, and test sets, hyperparameter tuning, and early stopping.
To handle the irregular time-interval readings of ambient sensors and enforce a consistent 1-minute temporal granularity, we applied two interpolation strategies.
First, for continuous features (temperature, light and humidity), we used AKIMA interpolation.
AKIMA [16], a locally adaptive piecewise cubic interpolation method, produced smoother trajectories while preserving the original directional trends and temporal dynamics of the sensor data.
text.formatted: AKIMA <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, a locally adaptive piecewise cubic interpolation method, produced smoother trajectories while preserving the original directional trends and temporal dynamics of the sensor data.

text.text: Moreover, our own pilot study found AKIMA interpolation also improved deep learning model performance when handling time-series sensors data [17].
text.formatted: Moreover, our own pilot study found AKIMA interpolation also improved deep learning model performance when handling time-series sensors data <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Second, for binary event-based sensors (motion and door), missing intervals were handled using zero-filling, reflecting the absence of activity or door closure events.

This strategy provides a more realistic representation of inactivity in sparse event streams and avoids biasing sequential models toward false positives (motion detected while there is no motion), ensuring temporal 1-minute consistent gap timeseries across heterogeneous sensor data fed to the deep learning models.
For each home, the minute-level sensor data were partitioned at the complete-calendarday level into mutually exclusive training, validation, and test sets.
The most recent days were reserved as the chronological test set, ensuring that all test observations occurred strictly after the development period comprising the training and validation sets.
This design approximated the intended prospective application, in which a model developed from previously collected sensor data is used to recognize activities on future, unseen days.
Training and validation days were selected exclusively from the earlier development period, with attention to maintaining activity representation and adequate coverage of less frequent classes.
All 10-, 30-, and 60-minute sequences were generated separately within their assigned days, and no sequence was permitted to cross a calendar-day or data-partition boundary.

This splitting strategy is more rigorous than randomly assigning individual observations or overlapping windows because temporally adjacent samples are highly correlated and can otherwise appear in both training and testing sets, producing optimistically biased performance estimates [18].

text.text: The validation set alone guided hyperparameter selection, early stopping, and model selection, whereas the held-out test set was used only for final performance estimation, consistent with established recommendations for prediction-model development and leakage prevention [19].

text.text: Robustness was further supported through class-weighted learning, dropout, weight decay, gradient clipping, restoration of the best validation checkpoint, deterministic random seeds, and reporting of per-class F1 and macro-AUC to account for class imbalance.

Importantly, identical partitions, preprocessing procedures, sequence lengths, model-selection criteria, and training settings were applied to the LSTM, Global Transformer, and Room-Aware Transformer, thereby improving the fairness and reproducibility of model comparisons.

Compared with conventional random or standard k-fold splitting, this design better preserves the temporal structure of continuous in-home sensing data and provides a more realistic estimate of within-home performance on future days, although it should not be interpreted as external validation across unseen homes or participants.

The three deep-learning architectures were trained using architecture-specific configurations appropriate to their distinct temporal-learning mechanisms, while shared experimental settings were standardized to facilitate direct comparison [14] [17] [18].

text.text: For the stacked unidirectional LSTM, input sequences of 10, 30, and 60 minutes were processed recurrently through stacked LSTM layers with predefined candidate hidden-state dimensions and layer depths.
We applied dropout between recurrent layers to reduce overfitting, and the final hidden-state representation was passed to a fully connected layer for multiclass ADL classification.

The global Transformer projected all sensor and temporal features jointly through a single embedding layer, added sinusoidal positional encodings, and processed the resulting representations using four encoder layers with four self-attention heads, GELU activation, feedforward dimensions equal to four times the embedding dimension, and dropout of 0.20.
In contrast, the room-aware transformer first grouped sensor features by functional-location prefixes.
Each group was processed through a dedicated linear projection, layer-normalization, GELU, and dropout branch, while hour, minute, and day-of-week variables were projected separately.

The room-specific and temporal embeddings were then concatenated, fused into a 16dimensional representation, combined with sinusoidal positional encodings, and processed through the same four-layer, four-head transformer encoder used by the global architecture before temporal mean pooling and ADL classification.

Across all three models, the same withinhome data partitions, upstream preprocessing workflow, sequence lengths, batch-sizes of 64 and 128, class-weighted cross-entropy loss, Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10³ and weight decay of 10, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, maximum of 100 epochs, and early stopping based on validation loss with a patience of 10 epochs were applied.
The same evaluation metrics were calculated for every architecture, and NumPy and PyTorch random seeds were fixed at 42 to reduce stochastic variation.

Model performances were evaluated on held-out test days using accuracy, per-class F1score, and micro-and macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC).

Accuracy quantified the overall proportion of correctly classified observations, while the per-class F1-score summarized activity-specific classification performance as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing false-positive and falsenegative errors.

ROC-AUC was calculated across the full range of classification thresholds, rather than at a fixed threshold of 0.5, and measured the model's ability to distinguish each ADL from competing classes [21].
text.formatted: ROC-AUC was calculated across the full range of classification thresholds, rather than at a fixed threshold of 0.5, and measured the model's ability to distinguish each ADL from competing classes <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Micro-AUC pooled one-versus-rest decisions across all observations and classes; consequently, it primarily reflected discrimination for prevalent activities such as Sleep/Rest, Leisure/Social, and Mobility from less prevalent activities.

In contrast, macro-AUC assigned equal weight to every activity-specific AUC, ensuring that less frequent but clinically meaningful ADLs, including Toileting/Continence and Dressing, contributed equally to the overall estimate, regardless of their support.

In summary, high micro-AUC indicated good overall population-level discrimination, whereas high macro-AUC demonstrated that performance was distributed more equitably across common and underrepresented activities.
Their joint interpretation prevented performance on dominant classes from obscuring weak recognition of infrequent ADLs, a well-established concern in imbalanced multiclass classification [9].

text.text: Per-class F1-score and AUC were additionally reported to identify specific activities for which favorable aggregate performance did not translate into reliable classification.
All models training and evaluation were conducted on a Linux Ubuntu 22.04 workstation running Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.5.1+cu121, and CUDA-enabled deep-learning libraries.
The system was equipped with a NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU.
Phase I compared LSTM and global transformer models using data from two adult volunteers (V1 and V2).
For V1, both architectures achieved similar average performance, with an accuracy of 0.72 and AUC of 0.94.

For V2, the transformer improved average accuracy from 0.51 to 0.59 and AUC from 0.86 to 0.89 relative to the LSTM, with the best transformer configuration reaching an accuracy of 0.64 and AUC of 0.91.

These findings established the feasibility of learning participant-specific ADL patterns from low-cost ambient sensor data and motivated Phase II, in which the approach was extended to five real-world homes involving participants with mild NCD.
Phase II evaluated both the global feature representation and the proposed room-aware Transformer to accommodate differences in home layouts, monitored rooms, and activity distributions.

However, its relative performance was less consistent for AUC-based discrimination.
The LSTM and the Global Transformer achieved competitive performance in micro-and macro-AUC.

text.text: Shorter, 10-minute windows frequently produced the highest discrimination, particularly for the LSTM and Room-Aware Transformer.

For example, the Room-Aware Transformer achieved its highest micro-AUC at 10 minutes in Homes A, D, and E (0.70, 0.80, and 0.65), while its highest macro-AUC also occurred at 10 minutes in Homes A, C, D, and E. The 30-minute window provided localized improvements, including the Room-Aware Transformer's highest accuracy and micro-AUC in Home B (0.51 and 0.82) and the LSTM's highest accuracy in Homes A, C, and E. In contrast, the 60-minute window was beneficial primarily for selected home-model combinations, including the Room-Aware Transformer's highest accuracy in Home A (0.37) and the Global Transformer's highest accuracy and micro-AUC in Home C (0.50 and 0.82).
Longer windows frequently reduced AUC performance, particularly in Home A, suggesting that additional temporal context did not consistently improve activity discrimination.
Overall, 10-minute windows were generally more effective for preserving short-term activity patterns, whereas the benefits of 30-and 60-minute windows were model-and home-specific.

This two-phase study evaluated LSTM, global Transformer, and room-aware Transformer architectures for participant-level ADL classification from ambient home sensors.
Phase I established feasibility in a pilot home.
Phase II compared the three architectures across five homes of adults with mild NCD using identical day-level partitions and 10-, 30-, and 60minute temporal windows.
The principal finding was not uniform superiority of one architecture.
Instead, the room-aware Transformer provided selective gains in accuracy in several homewindow settings, while the global Transformer produced marginally higher mean micro-AUC and macro-AUC.
Performance varied more by home, activity, and temporal context than the aggregate results alone would suggest.

Across the five homes and three temporal windows, the room-aware Transformer most often achieved the highest accuracy (8 of 15 settings), although its mean accuracy matched that of the global Transformer (0.43 for both).
A possible explanation for these selective gains is the room-aware architecture's explicit separation of room-specific feature extraction from temporal modeling.

Dedicated projection branches allow each room's sensor features to be transformed independently before fusion, preserving location-specific structure that the conventional LSTM must learn implicitly from jointly presented inputs.
Multi-head self-attention subsequently relates observations across the fused sequence, potentially supporting recognition of room transitions and temporally separated activity cues.

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, the evaluation included only five homes with 9 to 20 annotated days per home, limiting generalizability to other residents, layouts, routines, and sensor configurations.
The chronological day-level test design provides a realistic estimate of within-home performance on future days, but it is not external validation in unseen homes or participants.
Second, activity labels were based on structured aligned to minute-level intervals.
Despite staff review and follow-up clarification, retrospective reporting, uncertain activity boundaries, and incomplete logging may introduce label noise.
Third, substantial class imbalance and the absence of some activities from individual test sets limited reliable estimation for infrequent categories.
No Activity was particularly ambiguous because it could represent sedentary behavior or an unreported activity.

Fourth, each home included a co-resident caregiver, and ambient sensors cannot attribute motion or environmental changes to a specific person; models therefore predicted the participant's logged activity from household-level signals, which may add noise when the participant and caregiver were active in different rooms.

Fifth, results came from a single chronological split with 2 to 3 test days per home and a single random seed, without confidence intervals, so small between-model differences should be interpreted cautiously.
Finally, cognitive status was not reassessed throughout the analyzed periods, so possible changes in neurocognitive status were not modeled.
This study supports the feasibility of privacy-preserving, participant-level ADL recognition from ambient sensors in homes of adults with mild NCD.

The room-aware Transformer achieved favorable accuracy in selected home-window settings, particularly where spatial organization appeared informative, but it did not consistently exceed the global Transformer or LSTM across all metrics.
Sleep/Rest was recognized most reliably, whereas infrequent and ambiguous activities remained challenging.
The findings support further evaluation of spatially structured models using larger, more diverse samples, repeated uncertainty-aware experiments, and external validation in unseen homes.
Clinical use will require evidence that reliable activity recognition translates into meaningful longitudinal assessment and decision support.
